punctuated:
倫善〔貫廣東廣州府順德縣，民籍，國子生，治《詩經》，字國寶，行一，年四十二，七月初一日生〕。曾祖仕廣；祖景新；父尚琳；母張氏。慈侍下。弟嘉、啓、亶、喜、亷。娶廖氏。廣東鄉試第三十一名，會試第一百名。

陳睿〔貫福建泉州府惠安縣，民籍，縣學生，治《禮記》，字邦獻，行四，年三十五，三月十一日生〕。曾祖彦文；祖昂；父玧珪；嫡母張氏、杜氏；生母何氏。慈侍下。兄俊、嘉言、敏。娶何氏。福建鄉試第四十名，會試第二百七十七名。

滑浩〔貫浙江餘姚縣人，太醫院籍，國子生，治《禮記》，字宗源，行十六，年三十二，二月十九日生〕。曾祖伯仁；祖孟驥〔醫學訓科〕；父志鏞〔良醫正〕；母吳氏。具慶下。兄思讓、深、思述、思傑〔醫學訓科〕；弟思賢、瀚。娶夏氏，繼娶徐氏。順天府鄉試第一百十六名，會試第二百八十名。

唐昭〔貫河南開封府祥符縣，匠籍，國子生，治《詩經》，字文煥，行五，年三十五，十一月二十四日生〕。曾祖德祿；祖欽；父瑛；母馮氏。慈侍下。兄春、昱、晧、義；弟相、聰、時。娶楊氏。河南鄉試第三十一名，會試第二百九十三名。
translation_en:
Lun Shan 倫善 (native of Shunde County, Guangzhou Prefecture, Guangdong, of civilian registration; a National University Student specializing in the Classic of Poetry (Shijing); courtesy name Guobao, first in seniority among brothers, aged forty-two, born on the first day of the seventh month). His great-grandfather was Lun Shiguang 仕廣, his grandfather was Lun Jingxin 景新, his father was Lun Shanglin 尚琳, and his mother is née Zhang 張氏. His mother is living (cishixia). His younger brothers are Lun Jia 嘉, Lun Qi 啓, Lun Dan 亶, Lun Xi 喜, and Lun Lian 亷. He married née Liao 廖氏. He placed 31st in the Guangdong Provincial Examination and 100th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Chen Rui 陳睿 (native of Hui'an County, Quanzhou Prefecture, Fujian, of civilian registration; a County Student specializing in the Record of Rites (Liji); courtesy name Bangxian, fourth in seniority, aged thirty-five, born on the eleventh day of the third month). His great-grandfather was Chen Yanwen 彦文, his grandfather was Chen Ang 昂, his father was Chen Yungui 玧珪, his legal mothers were née Zhang 張氏 and née Du 杜氏, and his birth mother is née He 何氏. His mother is living (cishixia). His elder brothers are Chen Jun 俊, Chen Jiayan 嘉言, and Chen Min 敏. He married née He 何氏. He placed 40th in the Fujian Provincial Examination and 277th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Hua Hao 滑浩 (originally of Yuyao County, Zhejiang, registered under the Imperial Academy of Medicine; a National University Student specializing in the Record of Rites (Liji); courtesy name Zongyuan, sixteenth in seniority, aged thirty-two, born on the nineteenth day of the second month). His great-grandfather was Hua Boren 伯仁, his grandfather was Hua Mengji 孟驥 (Medical Prefectural Instructor), his father is Hua Zhiyong 志鏞 (Director of Princely Physicians), and his mother is née Wu 吳氏. Both of his parents are living (juqingxia). His elder brothers are Hua Sirang 思讓, Hua Shen 深, Hua Sishu 思述, and Hua Sijie 思傑 (Medical Prefectural Instructor); his younger brothers are Hua Sixian 思賢 and Hua Han 瀚. He married née Xia 夏氏, and after her took née Xu 徐氏 as his second wife. He placed 116th in the Shuntian Prefectural Provincial Examination and 280th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Tang Zhao 唐昭 (native of Xiangfu County, Kaifeng Prefecture, Henan, of artisan registration; a National University Student specializing in the Classic of Poetry (Shijing); courtesy name Wenhuan, fifth in seniority, aged thirty-five, born on the twenty-fourth day of the eleventh month). His great-grandfather was Tang Delu 德祿, his grandfather was Tang Qin 欽, his father was Tang Ying 瑛, and his mother is née Feng 馮氏. His mother is living (cishixia). His elder brothers are Tang Chun 春, Tang Yu 昱, Tang Hao 晧, and Tang Yi 義; his younger brothers are Tang Xiang 相, Tang Cong 聰, and Tang Shi 時. He married née Yang 楊氏. He placed 31st in the Henan Provincial Examination and 293rd in the Metropolitan Examination.

馮允中〔貫山東東昌府茌平縣民籍，縣學增廣生，治《詩經》，字信道，行一，年二十九，正月十五日生〕。曾祖彧〔主簿〕；祖文玉；父倫〔貢士〕；母陳氏。具慶下。弟一中。聘楊氏。山東鄉試第十八名，會試第二百八十八名。

吳淑〔貫直隸常州府宜興縣官籍，國子生，治《書經》，字艾夫，行二，年四十，正月三十日生〕。曾祖公達〔贈冬官正〕；祖復〔陰陽訓術〕；父蕢；母史氏。永感下。兄澤；弟淵、淮。娶殷氏。應天府鄉試第九十二名，會試第二百八十一名。

李德恢〔貫順天府東安縣民籍，縣學生，治《春秋》，字叔恢，行三，年三十，二月二十七日生〕。曾祖繼本〔翰林檢討〕；祖東〔行人司司副、贈太僕寺少卿〕；父侃〔右僉都御史〕；母張氏〔封恭人〕。嚴侍下。兄德容、德章〔貢士〕；弟德仁〔貢士〕。娶延氏。順天府鄉試第四十四名，會試第一百二十二名。

李毓〔貫山東武定州人，武功中衛匠籍，順天府學生，治《書經》，字鍾秀，行一，年三十五，四月二十三日生〕。曾祖善甫；祖子儀；父克用；母徐氏。慈侍下。弟珍、玘、諫、玟、瑭。娶郭氏，繼娶蔣氏。順天府鄉試第六十七名，會試第十名。
translation_en:
Feng Yunzhong 馮允中 (registered as a civilian householder in Chiping County, Dongchang Prefecture, Shandong; Added Student at the County School; specializing in the Classic of Poetry [Shijing]; courtesy name Xindao; first in generational seniority; age twenty-nine, born on the fifteenth day of the first month). His great-grandfather was Feng Yu (Assistant Magistrate); his grandfather was Feng Wenyu; his father is Feng Lun (Tribute Student); and his mother is née Chen. Both parents are living. His younger brother is Feng Yizhong. He is betrothed to a woman née Yang. He placed 18th in the Shandong Provincial Examination and 288th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Wu Shu 吳淑 (registered in an official household in Yixing County, Changzhou Prefecture, Southern Metropolitan Region [Zhili]; Student of the Directorate of Education; specializing in the Classic of History [Shujing]; courtesy name Aifu; second in generational seniority; age forty, born on the thirtieth day of the first month). His great-grandfather was Wu Gongda (posthumously honoured as Director of Winter Offices); his grandfather was Wu Fu (Instructor in the Prefectural Yin-Yang School); his father was Wu Kui; and his mother was née Shi. Both parents are deceased. His elder brother is Wu Ze, and his younger brothers are Wu Yuan and Wu Huai. He married a woman née Yin. He placed 92nd in the Yingtian Prefectural Provincial Examination and 281st in the Metropolitan Examination.

Li Dehui 李德恢 (registered as a civilian householder in Dong'an County, Shuntian Prefecture; County School Student; specializing in the Spring and Autumn Annals [Chunqiu]; courtesy name Shuhui; third in generational seniority; age thirty, born on the twenty-seventh day of the second month). His great-grandfather was Li Jiben (Examining Editor in the Hanlin Academy); his grandfather was Li Dong (Vice Director of the Messenger Office, posthumously honoured as Vice Minister of the Court of the Imperial Stud); his father is Li Kan (Right Assistant Censor-in-Chief); and his mother was née Zhang (invested as Respectful Lady). His father is living and his mother is deceased. His elder brothers are Li Derong and Li Dezhang (Tribute Student), and his younger brother is Li Deren (Tribute Student). He married a woman née Yan. He placed 44th in the Shuntian Prefectural Provincial Examination and 122nd in the Metropolitan Examination.

Li Yu 李毓 (a native of Wuding Subprefecture, Shandong, registered in an artisan household of the Central Guard of Martial Merit [Wugong Zhongwei]; Student of the Shuntian Prefectural School; specializing in the Classic of History [Shujing]; courtesy name Zhongxiu; first in generational seniority; age thirty-five, born on the twenty-third day of the fourth month). His great-grandfather was Li Shanfu; his grandfather was Li Ziyi; his father was Li Keyong; and his mother is née Xu. His mother is living and his father is deceased. His younger brothers are Li Zhen, Li Qi, Li Jian, Li Wen, and Li Tang. He married a woman née Guo, and took as his second wife a woman née Jiang. He placed 67th in the Shuntian Prefectural Provincial Examination and 10th in the Metropolitan Examination.

海澄〔貫廣東番禺縣人，海南衛軍籍，國子生，治《禮記》，字靜之，行一，嵗三十四，四月二十六日生〕。曾祖達；祖福寧；父方；母林氏。具慶下，弟深、潢、瀾、淵、浩、濟、潤、滄、渙、演、湛、泌、沂。娶麥氏。廣東鄉試第十六名，會試第十二名。

張鼐〔貫山東濟南府歷城縣民籍，國子生，治《易經》，字用和，行二，嵗三十三，九月二十六日生〕。曾祖敬中；祖獻〔光祿寺署丞〕；父諒〔陰陽正術〕；前母徐氏，母徐氏，繼母韓氏。慈侍下，兄鼎。娶翟氏。山東鄉試第五十二名，會試第一百二十一名。

雷以時〔貫河南汝寧府西平縣民籍，國子生，治《春秋》，字用中，行一，嵗三十九，三月初十日生〕。曾祖德；祖信；父溫；母田氏。具慶下，弟以元、以亨。娶王氏。河南鄉試第十四名，會試第一百六十五名。
translation_en:
Zhao Rang 趙讓 [registered in a civilian household of Tongxiang County, Jiaxing Prefecture, Zhejiang; a National University Student; specialized in the Classic of Documents (Shujing); courtesy name Yuanxun 元遜; second in seniority among his brothers; aged forty-one, born on the second day of the tenth month]. His great-grandfather was Zhao Lede 樂德; his grandfather was Zhao Zunli 遵禮; his father is Zhao Tinggui 廷珪; his mother was née Li 李氏, and his stepmother is née Yan 顏氏. Both his father and stepmother are living; he has an elder brother, Zhao Qian 謙, and younger brothers, Zhao Jin 謹, Zhao Cheng 誠, and Zhao Zi 諮. He married née Zhang 張氏. He placed 49th in the Zhejiang Provincial Examination and 286th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Hai Cheng 海澄 [a native of Panyu County, Guangdong, registered in a military household of the Hainan Guard; a National University Student; specialized in the Record of Rites (Liji); courtesy name Jingzhi 靜之; first in seniority among his brothers; aged thirty-four, born on the twenty-sixth day of the fourth month]. His great-grandfather was Hai Da 達; his grandfather was Hai Funing 福寧; his father is Hai Fang 方; his mother is née Lin 林氏. His great-grandfather was Ke Zhiren 志仁; his grandfather was Ke Yirong 以榮; his father is Ke Yi 義; his father's former wife was Lady Hong 洪氏; his birth mother was Lady Chen 陳氏; and his stepmother is Lady Shi 史氏. Both his father and stepmother are living. His younger brothers are Ke Shu 恕, Ke Hui 惠, Ke Mao 懋, and Ke Xian 憲. He married Lady Hu 胡氏. He placed 94th in the Yingtian Prefecture 應天府 Provincial Examination and 247th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Shi Tang 石瑭 [registered in Yuyao County 餘姚縣, Shaoxing Prefecture 紹興府, Zhejiang 浙江, under civilian registration; National University Student (guozisheng); specialized in the Record of Rites (Liji); courtesy name Tingjian 廷堅; fourth in seniority among brothers; aged thirty-eight, born on the twentieth day of the seventh month]. His great-grandfather was Shi Junshi 均實; his grandfather was Shi Shiying 世英; his father is Shi Wenbing 文秉; and his mother is Lady Yao 姚氏. Both his parents are living. His elder brothers are Shi Min 珉, Shi Lin 琳, and Shi Qi 玘; his younger brothers are Shi Xun 珣, Shi Lian 璉, Shi Cui 璀, Shi Jiu 玖, Shi Jin 瑾, and Shi Lin 璘. He married Lady Lu 盧氏. He placed 2nd in the Zhejiang Provincial Examination and 282nd in the Metropolitan Examination.

Zhang Fu 張輔 [registered in Yin County 鄞縣, Ningbo Prefecture 寧波府, Zhejiang 浙江, under civilian registration; National University Student (guozisheng); specialized in the Book of Documents (Shujing); courtesy name Yunzhong 允忠; second in seniority among brothers; aged twenty-nine, born on the thirteenth day of the second month]. His great-grandfather was Zhang Shen 慎; his grandfather was Zhang Yi 益 [Administration Vice Commissioner (canzheng) of Shandong 山東]; his father is Zhang [illegible]; and his mother is Lady Shi 施氏. Both his parents are living. His elder brother is Zhang Yue 軏; his younger brothers are Zhang Yi 軼, Zhang Jiao 較, Zhang Lan 讕, Zhang Gui 軌, Zhang Xuan 軒, Zhang Lun 輪, Zhang Zhe 轍, and Zhang Ke 軻. He married Lady Yang 楊氏. He placed 86th in the Zhejiang Provincial Examination and 13th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Zhang Xun 張勛 [registered in Wan County 完縣, Baoding Prefecture 保定府, Directly Attached (Zhili 直隸), under military registration; Added County Student (xianxue zengguangsheng); specialized in the Book of Odes (Shijing); courtesy name Jichang 紀常; first in seniority among brothers; aged twenty, born on the second day of the twelfth month]. His great-grandfather was Zhang Xi 喜 [recipient of an honorary cap and belt (guandai)]; his grandfather is Zhang Bin 彬 [Prefectural Director of Studies (jiaoshou)]; his father is Zhang Guan 官 [Government Student (shengyuan)]; and his mother is Lady Tian 田氏. Both his parents and grandparents are living. His younger brothers are Zhang Mai 勱 and Zhang Qin 勤. He married Lady Liu 劉氏. He placed 123rd in the Shuntian Prefecture 順天府 Provincial Examination and 73rd in the Metropolitan Examination.

His great-grandfather was Yunzhong 允中; his grandfather was Chenglie 承烈; his father is Zhoumian 周冕 [Confucian School Instructor (jiaoshou)]; and his mother is née Pi 皮. Both parents are living; he has an elder brother Xiang 翔 and a younger brother Yao 耀; he is married to née Chen 陳. He placed 16th in the Jiangxi Provincial Examination and 167th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Zhang Sui 張穟 [registered as a civilian household in Baoying County, Gaoyou Subprefecture, Yangzhou Prefecture, Southern Metropolitan Area (Zhili); National University Student; specializing in the Record of Rites (Liji); courtesy name Shimei 世美; first in generational seniority; age forty-three, born on the sixteenth day of the eleventh month]. His great-grandfather was Gucheng 穀成; his grandfather was Zhongren 仲仁; his father is Yanqing 彥清; his mother was née Tang 唐; and his stepmother is née Jiang 姜. His father and stepmother are both living; he has a younger brother Ji 稷 [Erudite in the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (taichang si boshi)]; he is married to née Zhao 趙. He placed 18th in the Yingtian Prefectural Provincial Examination and 77th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Li Xun 李遜 [registered as a civilian household in Yangxin County, Wuding Subprefecture, Jinan Prefecture, Shandong; National University Student; specializing in the Classic of Changes (Yijing); courtesy name Jingzhi 敬之; first in generational seniority; age thirty-five, born on the thirteenth day of the twelfth month]. His great-grandfather was Shiyuan 士原; his grandfather was Xian 顯; his father is Gui 貴; and his mother is née He 何. Both parents are living; he has younger brothers Shu 述 and Lian 連; he is married to née Yang 楊. He placed 16th in the Shandong Provincial Examination and 99th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Lin Yuanfu 林元甫 [registered as a military household in Putian County, Xinghua Prefecture, Fujian; Prefectural School Student; specializing in the Classic of History (Shujing); courtesy name Yuanfu 元甫; first in generational seniority; age thirty-one, born on the twelfth day of the sixth month]. His great-grandfather was Yuanzhen 原真; his grandfather was Hongtai 宏泰; his father is Liangbi 良弼; and his mother is née Huang 黃. Both parents are living; he has a younger brother Zhefu 哲甫; he is married to née Chen 陳. He placed 67th in the Fujian Provincial Examination and 36th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Liu Jing 劉璟 [native of Yanling County 鄢陵縣, Kaifeng Prefecture 開封府, Henan 河南, of civilian registration (minji); a County School Student (xian xuesheng) specializing in the Classic of Poetry (Shijing); courtesy name Dehui 德輝; first in seniority among brothers; aged thirty-one, born on the second day of the eighth month]. His great-grandfather was Liu Ju 聚; his grandfather was Liu Yi 義; his father is Liu Hai 海; his father's former wife was née Pan 潘氏, and his mother is née Duan 段氏. Both parents are living (juqing xia). His younger brothers are Liu Pei 珮 and Liu Zan 瓚. He married née Zhai 翟氏, and remarried née Wang 王氏. He placed thirty-sixth in the Henan Provincial Examination and one hundred ninety-third in the Metropolitan Examination.

Huang Yao 黃鑰 [native of Xiangshan County 香山縣, Guangzhou Prefecture 廣州府, Guangdong 廣東, of military registration (junji); an Added Student of the County School (xianxue zengguang sheng) specializing in the Classic of History (Shujing); courtesy name Shimei 世美; third in seniority among brothers; aged thirty-two, born on the twenty-seventh day of the twelfth month]. His great-grandfather was Huang Huasheng 華生; his grandfather was Huang Hongdao 宏道; his father was Huang Long 隆; his father's former wife was née Zhong 鍾氏, his birth mother was née Nie 聶氏, and his stepmother is née Chen 陳氏. His mother (or stepmother) is living (cishi xia). His elder brothers are Huang Jian 鑑 and Huang Yong 鏞, and his younger brothers are Huang Duo 鐸 and Huang Yue 鉞. He married née Zhao 趙氏. He placed seventy-third in the Guangdong Provincial Examination and one hundred fifty-sixth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Xu Hai 徐海 [native of Haining County 海寧縣, Hangzhou Prefecture 杭州府, Zhejiang 浙江, of military registration (junji); a Directorate Student (guozisheng) specializing in the Classic of Poetry (Shijing); courtesy name Jufu 鉅夫; second in seniority among brothers; aged thirty-eight, born on the thirteenth day of the eighth month]. His great-grandfather was Xu Yao 瑤; his grandfather was Xu Xiu 脩; his father was Xu Zhuo 拙; his mother is née Ping 平氏. His mother is living (cishi xia). His elder brother is Xu Jiang 江, and his younger brother is Xu Huai 淮. He married née Yang 楊氏. He placed fifty-seventh in the Zhejiang Provincial Examination and sixty-ninth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Li Ding 黎鼎 [native of Nanhai County 南海縣, Guangzhou Prefecture 廣州府, Guangdong 廣東, of military registration (junji); a Prefectural School Student (fu xuesheng) specializing in the Classic of Changes (Yijing); courtesy name Ruzhong 汝重; second in seniority among brothers; aged thirty-three, born on the tenth day of the tenth month]. His great-grandfather was Li Boying 伯英; his grandfather was Li Zhi'an 智安; his father is Li Hong 紘; his birth mother was née Huang 黃氏, and his stepmother is née Chen 陳氏. Both parents are living (juqing xia). His elder brother is Li Ang 昂, and his younger brothers are Li Mian 冕 and Li Gao 杲. He married née Zhou 周氏. He placed thirty-third in the Guangdong Provincial Examination and fifty-ninth in the Metropolitan Examination.

楊傑〔貫雲南大理府鄧川州民籍，州學生，治《詩經》，字獻夫，行二，年二十四，八月二十七日生〕。曾祖成，祖慧，父源，母羊氏。具慶下。兄俊〔聽選官〕，弟仁、信。娶杜氏。雲南鄉試第一名，會試第十七名。

唐瑢〔貫順天府宛平縣人，雲南雲南左衛官籍，國子生，治《易經》，字玉潤，行三，年三十八，十二月二十五日生〕。曾祖祐〔鎮撫〕，祖完〔鎮撫〕，父顯〔千戶〕，母梅氏〔封宜人〕。慈侍下。兄環〔千戶〕、玘，弟琳。娶汪氏。雲南鄉試第八名，會試第一百五十三名。

趙溥〔貫直隸常州府武進縣民籍，國子生，治《禮記》，字以周，行二，年四十四，七月二十日生〕。曾祖彥清，祖敏政，父叔震〔七品散官〕，母徐氏。慈侍下。兄昂〔訓導〕，弟宗立〔縣丞〕、宗繼〔同知〕、仲壽〔知州〕、以康。娶彭氏。順天府鄉試第九十二名，會試第二十二名。

劉英〔貫陝西盩厔縣人，錦衣衛官籍，國子生，治《詩經》，字廷用，行二，年四十，十一月初三日生〕。曾祖仲舒，祖本〔百戶〕，父義〔百戶〕，前母張氏〔贈宜人〕，母安氏。慈侍下。兄彬。娶王氏。順天府鄉試第三十九名，會試第一百二十六名。
translation_en:
Yang Jie 楊傑 (registered in a civilian household of Dengchuan Subprefecture 鄧川州, Dali Prefecture 大理府, Yunnan 雲南; a Subprefectural Student specializing in the Classic of Poetry [Shijing]; courtesy name Xianfu 獻夫, second in seniority among his brothers, aged twenty-four, born on the twenty-seventh day of the eighth month). His great-grandfather was Yang Cheng 楊成, his grandfather was Yang Hui 楊慧, his father is Yang Yuan 楊源, and his mother is Lady Yang 羊氏. Both of his parents are living. His elder brother is Yang Jun 楊俊 (Expectant Appointee), and his younger brothers are Yang Ren 楊仁 and Yang Xin 楊信. He married Lady Du 杜氏. He placed 1st in the Yunnan Provincial Examination and 17th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Tang Rong 唐瑢 (a native of Wanping County 宛平縣, Shuntian Prefecture 順天府, registered in an official household of the Yunnan Left Guard 雲南左衛 in Yunnan; a National University Student specializing in the Classic of Changes [Yijing]; courtesy name Yurun 玉潤, third in seniority, aged thirty-eight, born on the twenty-fifth day of the twelfth month). His great-grandfather was Tang You 唐祐 (Judge), his grandfather was Tang Wan 唐完 (Judge), his father was Tang Xian 唐顯 (Battalion Commander), and his mother is Lady Mei 梅氏 (invested as Lady of Suitability). His mother is living. His elder brothers are Tang Huan 唐環 (Battalion Commander) and Tang Qi 唐玘, and his younger brother is Tang Lin 唐琳. He married Lady Wang 汪氏. He placed 8th in the Yunnan Provincial Examination and 153rd in the Metropolitan Examination.

Zhao Pu 趙溥 (registered in a civilian household of Wujin County 武進縣, Changzhou Prefecture 常州府, Southern Metropolitan Area [Zhili 直隸]; a National University Student specializing in the Record of Rites [Liji]; courtesy name Yizhou 以周, second in seniority, aged forty-four, born on the twentieth day of the seventh month). His great-grandfather was Zhao Yanqing 趙彥清, his grandfather was Zhao Minzheng 趙敏政, his father was Zhao Shuzhen 趙叔震 (Honorary Official of the Seventh Rank), and his mother is Lady Xu 徐氏. His mother is living. His elder brother is Zhao Ang 趙昂 (Assistant Instructor), and his younger brothers are Zhao Zongli 趙宗立 (Vice Magistrate), Zhao Zongji 趙宗繼 (Vice Prefect), Zhao Zhongshou 趙仲壽 (Subprefect), and Zhao Yikang 趙以康. He married Lady Peng 彭氏. He placed 92nd in the Shuntian Prefectural Provincial Examination and 22nd in the Metropolitan Examination.

Liu Ying 劉英 (a native of Zhouzhi County 盩厔縣, Shaanxi 陝西, registered in an official household of the Embroidered-Uniform Guard 錦衣衛; a National University Student specializing in the Classic of Poetry [Shijing]; courtesy name Tingyong 廷用, second in seniority, aged forty, born on the third day of the eleventh month). His great-grandfather was Liu Zhongshu 劉仲舒, his grandfather was Liu Ben 劉本 (Company Commander), his father was Liu Yi 劉義 (Company Commander), his father's first wife was Lady Zhang 張氏 (posthumously honored as Lady of Suitability), and his mother is Lady An 安氏. His mother is living. His elder brother is Liu Bin 劉彬. He married Lady Wang 王氏. He placed 39th in the Shuntian Prefectural Provincial Examination and 126th in the Metropolitan Examination.

吳珍〔貫直隸沭陽縣人，遼東廣寧右衛軍籍，國子生，治《詩經》，字朝重，行四，年三十二，九月初三日生〕。曾祖安；祖昇；父智；母蘇氏。慈侍下。兄瑾、瑄、璜，弟琮、玥、琦。娶熊氏。山東鄉試第十三名，會試第一百二名。

馬昆〔貫浙江嘉興府平湖縣竈籍，國子生，治《詩經》，字克昌，行三，年三十六，九月初四日生〕。曾祖義；祖德；父驥；母胡氏。具慶下。兄昫、曙，弟昺、普、昇、晙、映、暕。娶朱氏。浙江鄉試第七十五名，會試第二百五十九名。
translation_en:
Li Can 李參 (native of Jiangyin County, Changzhou Prefecture, Southern Metropolitan Area [Zhili], of artisan household registration; National University Student specializing in the Classic of History [Shujing]; style name Suqing, second in seniority among brothers, aged thirty-seven, born on the twenty-seventh day of the seventh month). His great-grandfather was Li Yanji; his grandfather was Li Zhongyong; his father is Li Jian; and his mother is née Zhu. Both parents are living. He has an elder brother, Li Pei, and younger brothers, Li Kui and Li Fang. He is married to née Jiang. He ranked 56th in the Yingtian Prefectural Provincial Examination and 132nd in the Metropolitan Examination.

Chen Gu 陳轂 (native of Shanyin County, Shaoxing Prefecture, Zhejiang, of military household registration; National University Student specializing in the Record of Rites [Liji]; style name Tuishi, seventh in seniority among brothers, aged thirty-seven, born on the fifth day of the eleventh month). His great-grandfather was Chen Qing; his grandfather was Chen Jingwen; his father was Chen Duan [Assistant Magistrate]; his father's former wife was née Zhang; and his mother is née Ma. His mother is living. He has elder brothers Chen Yi, Chen Han, Chen Zhu, Chen Xi, and Chen Hao, and younger brothers Chen Yue and Chen Shi. He is married to née Zhou. He ranked 26th in the Zhejiang Provincial Examination and 46th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Wu Zhen 吳珍 (originally from Shuyang County, Southern Metropolitan Area [Zhili], registered in a military household of the Guangning Right Guard in Liaodong; National University Student specializing in the Classic of Poetry [Shijing]; style name Chaozhong, fourth in seniority among brothers, aged thirty-two, born on the third day of the ninth month). His great-grandfather was Wu An; his grandfather was Wu Sheng; his father was Wu Zhi; and his mother is née Su. His mother is living. He has elder brothers Wu Jin, Wu Xuan, and Wu Huang, and younger brothers Wu Cong, Wu Yue, and Wu Qi. He is married to née Xiong. He ranked 13th in the Shandong Provincial Examination and 102nd in the Metropolitan Examination.

Ma Kun 馬昆 (native of Pinghu County, Jiaxing Prefecture, Zhejiang, of saltern household registration; National University Student specializing in the Classic of Poetry [Shijing]; style name Kechang, third in seniority among brothers, aged thirty-six, born on the fourth day of the ninth month). His great-grandfather was Ma Yi; his grandfather was Ma De; his father is Ma Ji; and his mother is née Hu. Both parents are living. He has elder brothers Ma Xu and Ma Shu, and younger brothers Ma Bing, Ma Pu, Ma Sheng, Ma Jun, Ma Ying, and Ma Jian. He is married to née Zhu. He ranked 75th in the Zhejiang Provincial Examination and 259th in the Metropolitan Examination.

王珩〔貫直隸真定府趙州，民籍，國子生。治《書經》，字美器，行七，年二十八，十月十二日生〕。曾祖成甫；祖翥；父惟政；前母張氏，母張氏。具慶下。兄瑛、璽、瑄〔縣丞〕、璣、琮、琳，弟瓛、珙、璠。娶牟氏，繼娶劉氏。順天府鄉試第七十七名，會試第六十名。

translation_en:
Lin Zi 林資 (registered in Xiushui County, Jiaxing Prefecture, Zhejiang, under civilian household status; National University Student; specialized in the Classic of Documents; courtesy name Xingchu; second in seniority among brothers; age twenty-six; born on the ninth day of the second month). His great-grandfather was Lin Derun (invested as Secretary in the Ministry of War); his grandfather is Lin Mao (Prefect); his father is Lin Jie; and his mother is née Tang. Both his grandparents and parents are living. His elder brother is Lin Can, and his younger brother is Lin Zhi. He is married to née Xu. He placed forty-first in the Zhejiang Provincial Examination and two-hundredth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Guo Zi 郭資 (registered in Shanghang County, Tingzhou Prefecture, Fujian, under civilian household status; County Student; specialized in the Classic of Poetry; courtesy name Fengyuan; first in seniority among brothers; age thirty-eight; born on the second day of the fifth month). His great-grandfather was Guo Yuanzhong; his grandfather was Guo Bingshan; his father was Guo Jun; and his mother is née Chen. His mother is living. His younger brothers are Guo Zan and Guo He. He is married to née Zhang. He placed ninetieth in the Fujian Provincial Examination and one hundred forty-seventh in the Metropolitan Examination.

Wang Heng 王珩 (registered in Zhaozhou, Zhending Prefecture, Southern or Northern Metropolitan Area [Zhili], under civilian household status; National University Student; specialized in the Classic of Documents; courtesy name Meiqi; seventh in seniority among brothers; age twenty-eight; born on the twelfth day of the tenth month). His great-grandfather was Wang Chengfu; his grandfather was Wang Zhu; his father is Wang Weizheng; his father's former wife was née Zhang, and his mother is née Zhang. Both of his parents are living. His elder brothers are Wang Ying, Wang Xi, Wang Xuan (Vice Magistrate), Wang Ji, Wang Cong, and Wang Lin; his younger brothers are Wang Huan, Wang Gong, and Wang Fan. He married née Mou, and remarried née Liu. He placed seventy-seventh in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and sixtieth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Mao Fenglai 毛鳳来 (registered in Xiping County, Runing Prefecture, Henan, under civilian household status; Prefectural Student; specialized in the Classic of Documents; courtesy name Yingcheng; third in seniority among brothers; age twenty-five; born on the seventeenth day of the ninth month). His great-grandfather was Mao Gui; his grandfather was Mao Pengxiao (Department Magistrate); his father was Mao Xiang (Administration Vice Commissioner); his legal mothers were née Li and née Guo, and his birth mother is née Liao. His mother is living. His elder brothers are Mao Fengming (Tribute Student) and Mao Fengzhu (provincial graduate, juren); his younger brothers are Mao Fengqi and Mao Fengyang. He is married to née You. He placed twenty-second in the Henan Provincial Examination and two hundred twenty-fifth in the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en:
Ma Quan 馬銓 (registered in a military household of Nanhe County, Shunde Prefecture, Zhili; a National University Student specializing in the Classic of History (Shujing); courtesy name Bingheng; second in seniority among his brothers; aged twenty-nine, born on the fourth day of the first month). His great-grandfather was Ma Cai; his grandfather was Ma Ji (Prefectural Registrar); his father is Ma Zhen; his mother was née Jia, and his stepmother is née Zhu. Both his grandparents and parents are living. He has an elder brother, Yong, and younger brothers, Yue and Rui. He is married to née Diao. He placed 124th in the Shuntian Prefectural Provincial Examination and 134th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Yan Lun 閻倫 (registered in a military household of Xi County, Guangzhou, Runing Prefecture, Henan; a National University Student specializing in the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu); courtesy name Tianxu; first in seniority; aged twenty-nine, born on the twenty-second day of the fourth month). His great-grandfather was Yan Cheng; his grandfather was Yan Xin; his father was Yan Gui; his mother was née Zhu, and his stepmother is née Zhang. His mother is living while his father is deceased. He has younger brothers, Wei and Jun. He is married to née Ding. He placed 57th in the Henan Provincial Examination and 287th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Li Kui 李魁 (registered in a military household of Gaoyao County, Zhaoqing Prefecture, Guangdong; a National University Student specializing in the Classic of Changes (Yijing); courtesy name Shiyuan; first in seniority; aged twenty-eight, born on the twenty-seventh day of the twelfth month). His great-grandfather was Li Yanxiu; his grandfather was Li Bi; his father is Li He; and his mother is née Liu. Both of his parents are living. He has younger brothers, Taimao and Taisheng. He is married to née Ma. He placed 21st in the Guangdong Provincial Examination and 139th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Tian Jingxian 田景賢 (registered in a military household of Zhuozhou, Shuntian Prefecture; a Subprefectural Student specializing in the Classic of Poetry (Shijing); courtesy name Zongru; first in seniority; aged thirty-two, born on the second day of the second month). His great-grandfather was Tian Xingjian; his grandfather was Tian Wenzhi (posthumously titled Secretary in the Ministry of Revenue); his father was Tian Kuan; his father's first wife was née Li, and his mother is [illegible]. His mother is living while his father is deceased. He has younger brothers, Jing'ang, Jingzhe, Jingliang, and Jingming. He is married to [illegible]. He placed 74th in the Shuntian Prefectural Provincial Examination and 18[?]th in the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en:
Pan Sheng 潘盛 [originally from Zhejiang (six characters illegible), registered in an artisan household in Daxing County, Shuntian Prefecture; a National University Student specializing in the Classic of Changes (Yijing); style name Shilong, first in seniority among his brothers, aged thirty-two, born on the twenty-fourth day of the twelfth month]. His great-grandfather was Pan Zhongde, his grandfather was Pan Heng, his father is Pan Jun, and his mother is née Zhao. Both parents are living; he married née Zhou, and subsequently married née Guo. He placed seventy-ninth in the Shuntian Prefectural Provincial Examination and two hundred forty-eighth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Liu Qing 劉清 [registered in a military household in Yidu County, Qingzhou Prefecture, Shandong; a National University Student specializing in the Classic of Documents (Shujing); style name Konglian, first in seniority among his brothers, aged forty-four, born on the twenty-ninth day of the tenth month]. His great-grandfather was Liu Zundao, his grandfather was Liu Gongbi [posthumously honored as Director of a Bureau in the Ministry of Works], his father was Liu Yu [Prefect], and his mother was née Chen [invested as Lady of Suitability]. Both parents are deceased; his younger brother is Liu Liang, and he married née Dou and subsequently married née Huang. He placed sixth in the Shandong Provincial Examination and ninety-second in the Metropolitan Examination.

Zhang Yuanjie 張源潔 [registered in a civilian household in Min County, Fuzhou Prefecture, Fujian; an Added Student of the County School specializing in the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu); style name Xibai, fourth in seniority among his brothers, aged twenty-eight, born on the second day of the eighth month]. His great-grandfather was Zhang Xing [Police Chief], his grandfather is Zhang Ji, his father is Zhang Weiguan, his mother was née Lin, and his stepmother is née Wang. Both grandparents and parents are living; his elder brothers are Zhang Yuanqing [metropolitan graduate (jinshi)], Zhang Yuansu, and Zhang Yuansu, and he married née Zheng. He placed fourth in the Fujian Provincial Examination and eighty-seventh in the Metropolitan Examination.

Qin Sheng 秦昇 [registered in a civilian household in Nanchang County, Nanchang Prefecture, Jiangxi; a National University Student specializing in the Classic of Poetry (Shijing); style name Shuxi, seventh in seniority among his brothers, aged thirty-two, born on the first day of the second month]. His great-grandfather was Qin Qidi, his grandfather is Qin Benzhou, his father is Qin Jingbo, and his mother is née Deng. Both grandparents and parents are living; his elder brother is Qin Jing, his younger brothers are Qin Mian, Qin Xu, Qin Jin, Qin Chong, and Qin Chun, and he married née Li. He placed twelfth in the Jiangxi Provincial Examination and eleventh in the Metropolitan Examination.

title: 成化十一年進士登科錄
text:
皇帝制曰朕惟人君
奉
天子民治道所當先
者養與教也養民
莫重於制田里廣
===
樹畜教民莫大於
崇學校明禮義今
茲二者行之既久
而實效未臻于極
何歟豈任用未盡

punctuated: 皇帝制曰：朕惟人君奉天子民，治道所當先者，養與教也。養民莫重於制田里、廣樹畜；教民莫大於崇學校、明禮義。今茲二者，行之既久，而實效未臻于極，何歟？豈任用未盡
translation_en: The Emperor's decree reads: We reflect that for a ruler of men who upholds Heaven and treats the people as his children, what must come first in the Way of governance is nourishing and educating them. In nourishing the people, nothing is more important than regulating fields and village residences and expanding arboriculture and animal husbandry; in educating the people, nothing is greater than exalting schools and clarifying rites and righteousness. Now these two measures have been practiced for a long time, yet their actual results have not reached the utmost standard. Why is this? Could it be that in appointing officials We have not fully…

title: 成化十一年進士登科錄
text:
得人而替勸作興
之道有未至歟唐
虞三代田分井牧
之授學謹庠序之
訓當時民有恒產
===
士有恒心所以養
之教之者備矣其
良法美意皆後世
所當講者可厯舉
而言之歟若漢唐
alt_text:
得人而胥勸作興
之道有未至歟唐
虞三代田分井牧
之授學謹庠序之
訓當時民有恒產
===
士有恒心所以養
之教之者備矣其
良法美意皆後世
所當講者可歷舉
而言之歟若漢唐
punctuated: 得人，而替勸作興之道有未至歟？唐虞、三代，田分井牧之授，學謹庠序之訓，當時民有恒產，士有恒心，所以養之教之者備矣。其良法美意，皆後世所當講者，可厯舉而言之歟？若漢、唐、
translation_en: …the right men, or is it that the ways of encouraging and inspiring them have not yet reached perfection? In the eras of Yao and Shun (Tang Yu) and the Three Dynasties, fields were apportioned through the allotments of the well-field and pasture system, and learning was carefully maintained through the instruction of the community schools (xiang and xu). At that time, the common people had constant livelihoods and the scholars had constant minds; the means of nourishing and educating them were complete. Their fine methods and admirable intentions are all things that later generations ought to study—can you enumerate and discuss them one by one? As for the Han, Tang,…

臣謝遷
臣對臣聞為治之道固貴乎有仁民之政尤貴
乎有仁民之心盖仁心存於中而後仁政達於
外使有其心而無其政是謂徒善徒善不足以
為政有其政而無其心是謂徒法徒法不能以
自行先儒程子曰為政須要有綱紀文章又曰
必有關雎麟趾之意然後可以行周官之法度
此之謂也仁政本之仁心則内外兼舉本末不
遺而為治之道得矣尚何慮教養未備任用非
人而治效未臻其極耶唐虞三代所以治隆俗
===

非徒有其政而無其心歟欽惟
皇帝陛下以聖神文武之資紹
祖宗列聖之統恭己守成虚心圖治雖深居

欲皆歸於漸仁摩義之域是以
臨御之初他務未遑首

臣謝遷。

臣對：臣聞為治之道，固貴乎有仁民之政，尤貴乎有仁民之心。盖仁心存於中，而後仁政達於外。使有其心而無其政，是謂徒善，徒善不足以為政；有其政而無其心，是謂徒法，徒法不能以自行。先儒程子曰：「為政須要有綱紀文章。」又曰：「必有《關雎》、《麟趾》之意，然後可以行《周官》之法度。」此之謂也。仁政本之仁心，則内外兼舉，本末不遺，而為治之道得矣。尚何慮教養未備、任用非人，而治效未臻其極耶？唐、虞、三代所以治隆俗美者，以此心、此政也；漢、唐、宋所以治不古若者，豈非徒有其政而無其心歟？

欽惟皇帝陛下，以聖神文武之資，紹祖宗列聖之統，恭己守成，虚心圖治。雖深居九重之中，而念周四表之外。慮民生之或未厚，必欲皆安於飽食暖衣之天；慮民德之或未淳，必欲皆歸於漸仁摩義之域。是以臨御之初，他務未遑，首耕籍田，以示重農而務本；繼幸太學，以示尊道而崇儒。丕緒恢張，仁聞四達，
translation_en:
Your servant Xie Qian 謝遷.

Your servant replies: Your servant has heard that in the way of governance, while it is certainly important to have benevolent governance toward the people, it is even more important to have a benevolent heart toward the people. For only when a benevolent heart is preserved within can benevolent governance be extended without. If one has the heart but lacks the governance, this is called "goodness alone," and goodness alone is not sufficient for governance; if one has the governance but lacks the heart, this is called "laws alone," and laws alone cannot put themselves into practice. The former Confucian master Master Cheng (Chengzi 程子) said: "To govern, there must be overarching principles and institutional forms." He also said: "Only when there is the spirit of the Odes 'Cry of the Osprey' (Guanju 關雎) and 'Hoof of the Unicorn' (Linzhi 麟趾) can one implement the institutions of the Offices of Zhou (Zhouguan 周官)." This is what is meant. When benevolent governance is rooted in a benevolent heart, both the inner and the outer are upheld together, neither root nor branch is neglected, and the way of governance is attained. Why then would one still worry that instruction and nourishment are not yet complete, that appointments do not go to the right men, or that the efficacy of rule has not yet reached its peak? The reason that in the ages of Tang 唐, Yu 虞, and the Three Dynasties governance flourished and customs were admirable was because of this heart and this governance; the reason that under the Han 漢, Tang 唐, and Song 宋 governance did not match antiquity—was it not because they merely had the governance without the heart?

Your servant reverently reflects that Your Majesty the Emperor, endowed with sagely, divine, civil, and martial qualities, has succeeded to the line of the imperial ancestors and successive sage rulers, conducting Yourself with reverent self-restraint to preserve what has been achieved and keeping an open mind in planning for good governance. Though dwelling deep within the ninefold palace, Your thoughts encompass everything beyond the four reaches of the world. Concerned that the people's livelihood may not yet be abundant, You necessarily wish for all to rest secure in a world of full bellies and warm clothing; concerned that the people's morals may not yet be pure, You necessarily wish for all to return to a realm imbued with benevolence and polished by righteousness. Therefore, at the very beginning of Your reign, before finding leisure for other affairs, You first plowed the Sacred Field (jitian 籍田) to demonstrate the importance of agriculture and devotion to the root; next You visited the Directorate of Education (Taixue 太學) to demonstrate reverence for the Way and esteem for Confucian learning. The great patrimony has been expanded, Your benevolent reputation has reached in all four directions, …

text:
所謂寵綏四方而克相上帝者亦已至矣茲猶
以實效未臻其極而慮任用未盡得人乃進臣
等于
廷俯賜
清問講求至理必欲追復唐虞三代之盛此不自
滿假稽于有眾之盛心也夫內不自滿而外稽
于眾則何所為而不至其極哉
陛下真大有為之君可以為堯舜可以為禹湯文武
可以唐虞三代斯世也斯世斯民何其幸歟臣
雖庸陋敢不效一得之愚以對揚
===
明命之萬一乎竊惟天降下民作之君作之師君
所以治之師所以教之書曰民非后罔克胥匡
以生又曰克綏厥猷惟后信乎人君奉
天子民其為治之道莫大乎養與教也教養未盡不
足以言治故孔子之告冉有必曰富之教之孟
子之論王道教養之外亦無餘說誠以仁政不
外乎此耳然養莫重於制田里而教莫先於崇
不均樹畜不廣欲民生之遂得乎教莫先於崇
學校而明禮義學校不修禮義不明欲民性之
復得乎夫是二者固必由任用得其人而後實

punctuated:
所謂「寵綏四方」而「克相上帝」者，亦已至矣。茲猶以實效未臻其極，而慮任用未盡得人，乃進臣等于廷，俯賜清問，講求至理，必欲追復唐、虞、三代之盛。此不自滿假、稽于有眾之盛心也。夫內不自滿而外稽于眾，則何所為而不至其極哉？陛下真大有為之君，可以為堯、舜，可以為禹、湯、文、武，可以唐、虞、三代斯世也。斯世斯民，何其幸歟！臣雖庸陋，敢不效一得之愚，以對揚明命之萬一乎？

竊惟天降下民，作之君，作之師。君所以治之，師所以教之。《書》曰：「民非后，罔克胥匡以生。」又曰：「克綏厥猷惟后。」信乎，人君奉天子民，其為治之道，莫大乎養與教也。教養未盡，不足以言治。故孔子之告冉有，必曰「富之」、「教之」；孟子之論王道，教養之外，亦無餘說，誠以仁政不外乎此耳。然養莫重於制田里，而教莫先於崇不均，樹畜不廣，欲民生之遂，得乎？教莫先於崇學校而明禮義，學校不修，禮義不明，欲民性之復，得乎？夫是二者，固必由任用得其人，而後實
translation_en:
… what is meant by "graciously pacifying the four quarters" and "being able to assist the Lord on High" has indeed already reached its utmost. Yet now, still deeming that practical results have not reached their perfection and worrying that appointments have not entirely secured the right men, You have summoned Your servants to the Court, condescending to grant Your clear inquiries to investigate the ultimate principles of governance, determined to recover the flourishing state of Tang, Yu, and the Three Dynasties. This is the magnificent mind of one who is not self-satisfied and consults the multitude. Indeed, when inwardly one is not self-satisfied and outwardly one consults the multitude, what undertaking will not reach its perfection? Your Majesty is truly a ruler of great capability, able to become like Yao and Shun, able to become like Yu, Tang, Wen, and Wu, and able to make this age like Tang, Yu, and the Three Dynasties. How fortunate are this age and this people! Though Your servant is mediocre and rustic, how dare I not offer my humble, single insight so as to respond to and extol even one ten-thousandth of Your illustrious mandate?

I humbly reflect that Heaven sent down the people below, and made for them rulers and made for them teachers. The ruler is the means to govern them; the teacher is the means to instruct them. The Book of Documents (Shu) says: "Without a sovereign, the people cannot mutually assist one another to live." It also says: "He who can tranquillize their ways is the sovereign." Truly, when a ruler receives Heaven's mandate to treat the people as his children, in his way of governance there is nothing greater than nourishing and instructing! When instruction and nourishment are not fully realized, one cannot speak of governance. Therefore, when Confucius (Kongzi) advised Ran You, he necessarily spoke of "enriching them" and "instructing them"; when Mencius (Mengzi) discussed the Kingly Way, beyond instruction and nourishment he likewise had no further doctrine—truly because benevolent government is nothing other than this. Yet in nourishing, nothing is more important than regulating fields and village homesteads, while in instructing, nothing takes precedence over honoring [? text garbled: likely missing "schools, and if fields and homesteads"] are not equalized, and planting and animal husbandry are not widespread, if one wishes for the people's livelihood to be fulfilled, can it be achieved? In instructing, nothing takes precedence over honoring schools and clarifying ritual and righteousness; if schools are not maintained and ritual and righteousness are not clarified, and one wishes for the people's nature to be restored, can it be achieved? Now, these two matters must certainly depend upon appointing the right men, and only afterward can practical…

translation_en:
… practical results reach their utmost perfection. Yet if we trace this to its root and discuss it, it lies solely in the heart-and-mind of the ruler. Mencius said: "The former kings had hearts that could not bear to see the sufferings of others, and thus they had governments that could not bear to see the sufferings of others. When one carries out a government that cannot bear to see the sufferings of others with a heart that cannot bear to see the sufferings of others, bringing order to the world is as easy as turning it on one's palm." If a ruler lacks this heart-and-mind and merely busies himself with the trivialities of institutional regulations and detailed rules, then what he implements is not true governance and those whom he employs are not the right men; even if he wishes to speak of order, it is all merely perfunctory. Your servant begs to verify this from antiquity and set it forth for Your Majesty.

In the time of Tang [Yao] and Yu [Shun], when the waters and land were not yet pacified and the multitude of the people did not yet have grain to eat, the sage was worried by this; thereupon he appointed Qi (棄) as Prince Millet (Houji) to sow the hundred grains in season, and when the hundred grains ripened, the people were nourished. When they were well-fed and warmly clothed but lacked instruction, they were close to birds and beasts, and the sage was again worried by this; thereupon he appointed Xie (契) as Minister of Education (Situ) to reverently spread the five teachings, and when the five teachings were spread, the hundred surnames grew affectionate toward one another.

In the time of the Three Dynasties, as for their nourishing of the people: the Xia dynasty allotted fifty mu and used the tribute (gong) system, the Yin people allotted seventy mu and used the aid (zhu) system, and the Zhou people allotted one hundred mu and used the share (che) system. As for their instructing of the people: the schools of Xia were called xiao, the schools of Yin were called xu, and the schools of Zhou were called xiang. Speaking in terms of when these institutions reached their utmost completeness, in the allotment of fields and lands, the "well" (jing) and "pasture" (mu) units differed in their regulations; in the establishment of schools, the lesser and greater learning differed in their instruction. For instance, in flat and fertile lands, one hundred mu constituted a household allotment (fu), and nine allotments made one well-field (jing); in low-lying and marshy lands, nine allotments made a pasture unit (mu), and two pasture units equaled one well-field. Such was the completeness of the well and pasture system whereby the people were nourished. At the age of eight, one entered the Elementary Learning (xiaoxue) and was taught the etiquette of sprinkling and sweeping, answering and replying, and advancing and withdrawing, as well as the polite arts of rites, music, archery, charioteering, calligraphy, and mathematics; at the age of fifteen, one entered the Great Learning (daxue) and was taught the arts of fathoming principle and rectifying the mind, and the ways of cultivating oneself and governing others. text:
使長入而使治皆剛簡直寬之德俊造秀乂之
士是以民有恒產而無啼饑號寒者矣士有恒
性而無放僻邪侈者矣然則其政立于上而效
成于下孰謂不本於得人又孰謂不本於君心
之仁乎質之經訂之傳而觀之則堯之兢兢舜
之業業固一憂民之心也禹之孜孜湯之慄慄
亦一憂民之心也至於文王之純亦不已武王
之永言配命又何嘗一念不在於民乎此其良
法美意固卓乎不可尚已古道既遠聖王不作
阡陌之端開而井田之制廢養民已無政矣坑
===
焚之禍作而詩書之習泯教民已無政矣又豈
有所謂仁民之心乎後世願治之君若漢之文
明唐之太宗宋之太祖亦嘗留意於教養或躬
耕籍田而減租以勸農或口分世業而節費以
裕民或遣官度田而課民以種植養民之政有
矣然不過法制之虛文或尊師重傅而臨雍拜
老或大召名儒而增廣生員或增葺國學之祠
宇而親製孔顏之贊詞教民之政有矣然不過
太平之粉飾究其存心果有如堯舜禹湯文武
之切於憂民者乎上既無堯舜禹湯文武之君

punctuated: 使長，入而使治，皆剛簡直寬之德、俊造秀乂之士。是以民有恒產，而無啼饑號寒者矣；士有恒性，而無放僻邪侈者矣。然則其政立于上而效成于下，孰謂不本於得人？又孰謂不本於君心之仁乎？質之經、訂之傳而觀之，則堯之兢兢、舜之業業，固一憂民之心也；禹之孜孜、湯之慄慄，亦一憂民之心也；至於文王之純亦不已、武王之永言配命，又何嘗一念不在於民乎？此其良法美意，固卓乎不可尚已。古道既遠，聖王不作，阡陌之端開而井田之制廢，養民已無政矣；坑焚之禍作而《詩》《書》之習泯，教民已無政矣。又豈有所謂仁民之心乎？後世願治之君，若漢之文、明，唐之太宗，宋之太祖，亦嘗留意於教養。或躬耕籍田而減租以勸農，或口分世業而節費以裕民，或遣官度田而課民以種植，養民之政有矣，然不過法制之虛文；或尊師重傅而臨雍拜老，或大召名儒而增廣生員，或增葺國學之祠宇而親製孔、顏之贊詞，教民之政有矣，然不過太平之粉飾。究其存心，果有如堯、舜、禹、湯、文、武之切於憂民者乎？上既無堯、舜、禹、湯、文、武之君，
translation_en:
… serve as leaders abroad or govern at home were all men possessing the virtues of firmness, simplicity, uprightness, and magnanimity, and scholars of outstanding talent, accomplishment, and refinement. Therefore, the common people had constant livelihoods and none cried out from hunger or wailed from cold; the scholars had constant moral nature and none indulged in unrestrained, perverse, depraved, or extravagant behavior. This being so, when governance was established above and its results were achieved below, who could say this was not rooted in obtaining the right men? And who could say it was not rooted in the benevolence of the ruler's heart?

If we verify this against the Classics and examine it through the commentaries, then the cautious vigilance of Yao and the fearful circumspection of Shun were indeed a single mind of concern for the people; the tireless diligence of Yu and the reverent awe of Tang were likewise a single mind of concern for the people; and as for King Wen's unceasing purity and King Wu's eternal accord with the Mandate, when was there ever a single thought not resting upon the people? Their fine laws and admirable intentions were indeed lofty and unsurpassed!

Once the ancient Way receded into the distance and sage-kings no longer arose, the system of field ridges and paths was opened up and the well-field institutions were abolished, so that there was no longer any governance for nourishing the people; the calamities of burying scholars alive and burning books broke out and the study of the Odes and the Documents was extinguished, so that there was no longer any governance for educating the people. How then could there be what is called a heart of benevolence toward the people?

In later ages, rulers who desired good governance—such as Emperors Wen and Ming of the Han, Emperor Taizong of the Tang, and Emperor Taizu of the Song—also paid attention to education and nourishment. Some personally plowed the sacred field and reduced land taxes to encourage agriculture; some instituted personal-share and hereditary-land allotments and curtailed expenditures to enrich the people; some dispatched officials to survey the fields and assessed the people on their planting and cultivation. Governance for nourishing the people did exist, yet it was nothing more than the empty letter of laws and regulations. Some honored teachers and esteemed tutors, visiting the Imperial University (Biyong) to pay respects to the aged; some summoned renowned Confucians in large numbers and expanded the quotas for students; some enlarged and repaired the shrines of the National University and personally composed eulogies for Confucius and Yan Hui. Governance for educating the people did exist, yet it was nothing more than window-dressing for an era of peace. If we examine the intentions they harbored, did they truly have such earnest concern for the people as Yao, Shun, Yu, Tang, King Wen, and King Wu? Since above there were no rulers like Yao, Shun, Yu, Tang, King Wen, and King Wu, …

text:
則奉承宣布者亦未必皆稷契伊周之臣是以
治效之著雖或至於海內富庶路不拾遺戶口
繁益求如古之畊田鑿井出作入息而不知帝
力何有則未也雖或至於黎民醇厚死囚来歸
道學可稱求如古之人人君子比屋可封而但
知順帝之則則未也此漢唐宋之所以不唐虞
三代也歟仰惟我
朝
列聖相承心堯舜禹湯文武之心行堯舜禹湯文武
之政必求復唐虞三代之治是以百紀修明庶
===
務振舉而於教養二事尤致重焉田雖無井牧
之異制然兼併有禁荒蕪有罰既有守令以司
之矣又兼
命藩臬以董之養民何以加焉學雖無庠序之異
制然廩餼有常廢墜有戒既有師儒以職之矣

punctuated:
則奉承宣布者，亦未必皆稷、契、伊、周之臣。是以治效之著，雖或至於海內富庶、路不拾遺、戶口繁益，求如古之畊田鑿井、出作入息，而不知帝力何有，則未也；雖或至於黎民醇厚、死囚来歸、道學可稱，求如古之人人君子、比屋可封，而但知順帝之則，則未也。此漢、唐、宋之所以不唐、虞、三代也歟！

仰惟我朝列聖相承，心堯、舜、禹、湯、文、武之心，行堯、舜、禹、湯、文、武之政，必求復唐、虞、三代之治。是以百紀修明，庶務振舉，而於教養二事尤致重焉。田雖無井牧之異制，然兼併有禁，荒蕪有罰，既有守令以司之矣，又兼命藩臬以董之，養民何以加焉？學雖無庠序之異制，然廩餼有常，廢墜有戒，既有師儒以職之矣，又專命憲臣以蒞之，教民何以加焉？良法美意，昭昭乎日月之照臨；深仁厚澤，蕩蕩乎天地之涵育。此我朝之治所以度越前古也。
translation_en:
… then those who received and promulgated their orders were not necessarily all ministers like Hou Ji, Xie, Yi Yin, and the Duke of Zhou. Therefore, in the manifestation of their governance, even though they sometimes reached the point where the realm within the seas was rich and populous, no one picked up lost articles on the roads, and the number of households multiplied, if one seeks the state of antiquity—where people plowed the fields and dug wells, went out to work at sunrise and came in to rest at sunset, not knowing what the sovereign's power had to do with them—that was not yet achieved. And even though they sometimes reached the point where the common people were simple and honest, condemned prisoners returned voluntarily, and Learning of the Way was praiseworthy, if one seeks the state of antiquity—where everyone was a gentleman, every household could be enfeoffed for virtue, and people effortlessly followed the sovereign's pattern—that too was not yet achieved. Is this not why the Han, Tang, and Song failed to equal Tang, Yu, and the Three Dynasties?

Looking up in reverence, the successive Sacred Emperors of our dynasty have inherited the throne one after another, taking the minds of Yao, Shun, Yu, Tang, King Wen, and King Wu as their own mind, and practicing the governance of Yao, Shun, Yu, Tang, King Wen, and King Wu, resolved to restore the order of Tang, Yu, and the Three Dynasties. Thus all the regulations are well-ordered and clear, general affairs are invigorated, and particular importance is placed upon the two matters of moral instruction and material nourishment. Although the fields do not have the distinct institutions of the well-field and pasture divisions, annexation of land is forbidden and leaving land uncultivated is penalized; not only are there prefects and magistrates to take charge of this, but provincial administration and surveillance commissioners are also concurrently commanded to supervise it—what more could be added to the nourishment of the people? Although the schools do not have the distinct institutions of the ancient xiang and xu academies, stipends of grain are regular and warnings are issued against neglect; not only are there instructors and Confucian scholars to hold office over them, but censorial officials are also specially commanded to oversee them—what more could be added to the instruction of the people? Good laws and fine intentions shine brightly like the illumination of the sun and moon; deep benevolence and generous grace are vast and boundless like the nurturing of Heaven and Earth. This is why the governance of our dynasty surpasses all previous antiquity.

title: 成化十一年進士登科錄
text:
陛下遠宗帝王之道近守
祖宗之法教養之政重加之意蓋無一念不在是也
伏讀
聖制有曰
朕承
祖宗大統撫臨億兆于茲有年夙夜兢惕弗遑寧處
期于家給人足教行刑措禮樂興而風俗美躋
斯世於雍熙泰和之盛果何道以致之歟即此
一念臣已知
陛下仁民無窮之心蓋不以目前之治而自已也
===
陛下撫盈成之運當鼎盛之年有可為之時有可為
之勢又有能為之資誠欲復隆古之治不過始
終此心焉耳始終此心則始終此治易曰聖人
久於其道而天下化成是知為治之道固未可
見小而欲速也且天下之大兆民之廣必人人
皆遂飽暖之願而後可以為養之至使有一民
不遂其生猶未也必人人皆歸禮義之化而後
可以為教之至使有一民不協于中猶未也方
今天下之民安於田里而生生自庸者固多矣
然而水旱相仍則展轉溝壑而無告者不惟見

punctuated: 陛下遠宗帝王之道，近守祖宗之法，教養之政重加之意，蓋無一念不在是也。伏讀聖制，有曰：「朕承祖宗大統，撫臨億兆，于茲有年，夙夜兢惕，弗遑寧處。期于家給人足，教行刑措，禮樂興而風俗美，躋斯世於雍熙泰和之盛，果何道以致之歟？」即此一念，臣已知陛下仁民無窮之心，蓋不以目前之治而自已也。陛下撫盈成之運，當鼎盛之年，有可為之時，有可為之勢，又有能為之資。誠欲復隆古之治，不過始終此心焉耳。始終此心，則始終此治。《易》曰：「聖人久於其道，而天下化成。」是知為治之道，固未可見小而欲速也。且天下之大，兆民之廣，必人人皆遂飽暖之願，而後可以為養之至；使有一民不遂其生，猶未也。必人人皆歸禮義之化，而後可以為教之至；使有一民不協于中，猶未也。方今天下之民，安於田里而生生自庸者，固多矣；然而水旱相仍，則展轉溝壑而無告者，不惟見
translation_en:
Your Majesty takes as Your distant model the Way of the ancient emperors and kings, and closely upholds the laws of the Imperial Ancestors. You attach redoubled importance to the administration of education and nourishment; indeed, there is not a single thought of Yours that does not rest upon this. Humbly reading the Imperial question, it says: "We have succeeded to the great heritage of Our Imperial Ancestors and have pacified and ruled over the hundreds of millions of people for some years now. Morning and night We are cautious and fearful, having no leisure to rest in peace. We hope that every household be well-supplied and every person content, that instruction prevail and punishments be set aside, that rites and music flourish and customs become virtuous, raising this world to the splendor of harmonious prosperity and supreme peace—by what Way indeed can this be brought about?" From this single thought alone, Your servant already knows Your Majesty's boundless heart of benevolence toward the people, and that You do not content Yourself and stop with the good governance currently before our eyes.

Your Majesty presides over an era of abundant fulfillment and is in the prime of life; You have the opportune time to act, the positional authority to act, and furthermore the natural endowments capable of acting. If You truly wish to restore the governance of high antiquity, it is nothing more than maintaining this mind from beginning to end. To maintain this mind from beginning to end is to maintain this governance from beginning to end. The Book of Changes (Yi) says: "The sage perseveres long in his Way, and all under Heaven is transformed and perfected." From this we know that in the Way of governance, one certainly must not look to petty results or desire quick success. Moreover, given the vastness of the Empire and the multitude of the millions of people, only when every single person fulfills their wish for full stomachs and warm clothes can nourishment be considered to have reached its utmost; if even a single person fails to fulfill their livelihood, it is not yet so. Only when every single person turns to the transformation of ritual and righteousness can education be considered to have reached its utmost; if even a single person does not conform to the Mean, it is not yet so. At present, among the people of the Empire, those who rest secure in their fields and villages and sustain themselves through their ordinary livelihoods are certainly many; yet when floods and droughts follow one upon another, those who roll into ditches and gullies with no one to appeal to are seen not only…

陛下養民之仁誠能久而不替田里未均必思所以

入阡陌勸課農桑如召信臣者乎既得其人又
===
假以歲月而考其功因其功而進退之則人孰
不思所以自勉而盡養民之職哉如此而家不
給人不足無是理也天下之民習於行義而熙
熙相安者固多矣然而饑饉荐臻則犬鼠偷竊
而無藉者不惟見於遐陬僻壤之所而名鄉廣
市亦有之如此而謂之教化洽未可也司風教
者方且溺於宴安而視教化為繁文恬不知所
以振勵轉移之術此猶未免貽

熙相安者固多矣然而饑饉荐臻則犬鼠偷竊
而無藉者不惟見於遐陬僻壤之所而名鄉廣
市亦有之如此而謂之教化洽未可也司風教
者方且溺於宴安而視教化為繁文恬不知所
以振勵轉移之術此猶未免貽
宸衷之憂也
陛下教民之仁誠能久而不怠學校必修不使有傾
punctuated: 於窮簷蔀屋之下，而通都大郡亦有之，如此而謂之生養遂，未可也。司民牧者方且急於催科，而視農桑為末務，漫不知所以撫字賑救之方，此猶未免動聖心之慮也。陛下養民之仁誠能久而不替，田里未均必思所以均之，樹畜未廣必思所以廣之，禁游手游食之蠹，懲橫斂苛征之虐，慎選循良愷悌之人以充守令之職。縱未必盡得如稷之賢，獨不可得出入阡陌、勸課農桑如召信臣者乎？既得其人，又假以歲月而考其功，因其功而進退之，則人孰不思所以自勉而盡養民之職哉？如此而家不給、人不足，無是理也。天下之民習於行義而熙熙相安者固多矣，然而饑饉荐臻，則犬鼠偷竊而無藉者，不惟見於遐陬僻壤之所，而名鄉廣市亦有之，如此而謂之教化洽，未可也。司風教者方且溺於宴安，而視教化為繁文，恬不知所以振勵轉移之術，此猶未免貽宸衷之憂也。陛下教民之仁誠能久而不怠，學校必修，不使有傾
translation_en:
…under wretched eaves and in thatched hovels, and they are even found in great metropolises and large commanderies. Under such circumstances, one cannot yet say that the people's livelihood and nourishment have been fulfilled. Those in charge of shepherding the people are meanwhile pressing urgently with tax collection while regarding agriculture and sericulture as secondary matters, completely ignorant of the methods for comforting, nurturing, and relieving the distressed. This still cannot avoid stirring concern in the Sacred Mind. If Your Majesty's benevolence in nourishing the people can truly endure without flagging—where fields and homesteads are not yet equalized, surely considering how to equalize them; where arboriculture and animal husbandry are not yet widespread, surely considering how to expand them; prohibiting the parasites who idle their hands and eat without working; punishing the tyranny of arbitrary exactions and harsh levies; and carefully selecting upright, capable, and amiable men to fill the posts of Prefect and Magistrate—even if we cannot always obtain worthies like Ji 稷, could we not at least find men like Shao Xinchen 召信臣, who went out among the field paths to encourage and supervise farming and sericulture? Once such men are obtained, if you also grant them sufficient years and months to examine their achievements, and promote or demote them on the basis of those achievements, then who would not think of exerting himself to fulfill the duty of nourishing the people? That families should still go unprovided for and people remain in want under such conditions is impossible in principle.

Among the people of the empire, those who are accustomed to practicing righteousness and live together in harmonious peace are certainly many. Yet when famines repeatedly occur, those with nothing to rely on who steal like dogs and rats are seen not only in remote corners and isolated regions, but also in renowned townships and broad marketplaces. Under such circumstances, one cannot yet say that moral transformation through instruction has become pervasive. Those in charge of public morals and instruction are meanwhile indulging in leisure and ease while regarding moral instruction as mere elaborate formality, quite unconcerned with the arts of rousing, encouraging, and transforming the people. This still cannot avoid leaving anxiety in the Imperial Heart. If Your Majesty's benevolence in instructing the people can truly endure without slackening—ensuring that schools are kept in repair so that they do not suffer the peril of…

title: 成化十一年進士登科錄
text:
頽之患禮義必明不使有壞亂之習禁惑世誣
民之言革驕淫侈僭之俗慎擇端方謹厚之士
以充師儒之任縱未必盡得如契之賢獨不可
得學兼體用封植人才如胡安定者乎既得其
人又重厥責任而考其績因其績而黜陟之則
人孰不思所以自効而盡教民之職哉如此而
教不行刑不措無是理也治既至於家給人足
教行刑措則禮樂以興風俗以厚四夷於是而
咸賓萬邦於是而寧謐諸福之物可致之祥莫
不畢集而雍煕泰和之隆復見於今日矣唐虞
===
三代豈得專美於前哉夫治效之所以隆固皆
本乎
陛下之一心然易逸難制者莫人心若也況人君之
心攻之者衆若聲色若貨利若遊畋方技土木
之類皆足以蠱惑揺蕩之者也苟非識見之明
而持守之堅者未必不為所移此心少移則人
欲日熾天理日消而無所不至矣是故動一侈
心則取民不以制而養民之政以廢動一躁心
則接下不以禮而教民之政以壞
陛下天資高邁志意堅定諒必能持守此心而慎終

punctuated:
頽之患，禮義必明，不使有壞亂之習。禁惑世誣民之言，革驕淫侈僭之俗，慎擇端方謹厚之士以充師儒之任。縱未必盡得如契之賢，獨不可得學兼體用、封植人才如胡安定者乎？既得其人，又重厥責任而考其績，因其績而黜陟之，則人孰不思所以自効而盡教民之職哉？如此而教不行、刑不措，無是理也。治既至於家給人足，教行刑措，則禮樂以興，風俗以厚，四夷於是而咸賓，萬邦於是而寧謐，諸福之物、可致之祥，莫不畢集，而雍煕泰和之隆，復見於今日矣，唐虞三代豈得專美於前哉？

夫治效之所以隆，固皆本乎陛下之一心。然易逸難制者，莫人心若也。況人君之心，攻之者衆，若聲色，若貨利，若遊畋、方技、土木之類，皆足以蠱惑揺蕩之者也。苟非識見之明而持守之堅者，未必不為所移。此心少移，則人欲日熾，天理日消，而無所不至矣。是故動一侈心，則取民不以制，而養民之政以廢；動一躁心，則接下不以禮，而教民之政以壞。陛下天資高邁，志意堅定，諒必能持守此心而慎終
translation_en:
… collapse and dilapidation, and ritual propriety and righteousness must be made clear, not allowing corrupt and disorderly customs to exist. Prohibit words that delude the world and deceive the people, reform customs of arrogance, licentiousness, extravagance, and usurpation, and carefully select upright, square, cautious, and generous scholars to fill the posts of Confucian teachers. Even if we cannot necessarily obtain men who are all as worthy as Xie, could we not at least obtain men whose learning combines substance and practical application and who nurture talent like Hu Anding (Hu Yuan 胡瑗)? Once such men are obtained, if you further give weight to their responsibilities, examine their achievements, and demote or promote them on the basis of those achievements, then who would not think of how to exert himself and fulfill the duty of educating the people? If this is done, there is no principle by which education would not take effect and punishments would not be set aside. Once governance reaches the point where every household is provided for and every person has enough, where education takes effect and punishments are set aside, then rites and music will flourish by this means, customs will grow generous by this means, the four surrounding non-Chinese peoples will thereupon all submit as guests, the myriad states will thereupon be tranquil and peaceful, all auspicious things and attainable omens of good fortune will gather without exception, and the flourishing of harmonious brightness and supreme peace will be seen again today! How could Tang (Yao), Yu (Shun), and the Three Dynasties monopolize such splendor in the past?

Now, that by which the efficacy of governance flourishes is assuredly rooted entirely in the single mind of Your Majesty. Yet nothing is easier to let stray or harder to control than the human mind. How much more is this true of the ruler's mind, which is assailed by many things! Things such as music and women, goods and profit, excursions and hunting, magical arts and technical skills, and construction projects are all sufficient to bewitch, delude, shake, and unsettle it. Unless one possesses clear insight and firm self-command, one will not necessarily avoid being swayed by them. If this mind is swayed even slightly, then human desires will blaze more fiercely day by day, Heavenly Principle will diminish day by day, and there is nothing to which it will not lead. Therefore, if a single extravagant impulse is stirred, extractions from the people will not follow the regulations, and the governance of nourishing the people will thereby be abandoned; if a single impatient impulse is stirred, subordinates will not be treated with ritual propriety, and the governance of educating the people will thereby be ruined. Your Majesty's natural endowment is lofty and surpassing, and your will and intentions are firm and settled; surely you will be able to hold fast to this mind and be as careful at the end…

title: 成化十一年進士登科錄
text:
如始矣然以成湯之聖每致警於盤銘之辭武
王之聖恒究心於丹書之戒學問之功其可以
少緩乎先儒范氏有言人君之心惟在所養
陛下欲致帝王之治烏可不求帝王養心之術
國朝經筵之設宸為近古左經右史朝講暮讀聞
於耳接於目而優游浸漬於心則所以防非窒
慾而長善者莫要於此臣領
陛下日御
經筵進講不輟毋視之為虛文毋應之以故事俾
賢士大夫常侍列於前後左右從容燕閒紬繹
===
陳說所聞者必善言所見者必善行于以涵養
此心以不失其本然之天充廣此心以不虧其
固有之量則養民教民之政亦將始終無間而
治效愈久愈盛矣天下治忽之幾端在乎此臣
學術疎淺荷
朝廷教養有年其於古昔聖賢格心之學亦嘗聞
其大槩矣故敢陳此以上酬
陛下求言之盛心也伏願
留神省覽則天下幸甚臣干冒
天威不勝戰慄之至臣謹對

punctuated: 如始矣。然以成湯之聖，每致警於《盤銘》之辭；武王之聖，恒究心於《丹書》之戒。學問之功，其可以少緩乎？先儒范氏有言：「人君之心，惟在所養。」陛下欲致帝王之治，烏可不求帝王養心之術？國朝經筵之設，宸為近古。左經右史，朝講暮讀，聞於耳，接於目，而優游浸漬於心，則所以防非窒慾而長善者，莫要於此。臣領陛下日御經筵，進講不輟，毋視之為虛文，毋應之以故事，俾賢士大夫常侍列於前後左右，從容燕閒，紬繹陳說，所聞者必善言，所見者必善行，于以涵養此心，以不失其本然之天，充廣此心，以不虧其固有之量，則養民教民之政，亦將始終無間，而治效愈久愈盛矣。天下治忽之幾，端在乎此。臣學術疎淺，荷朝廷教養有年，其於古昔聖賢格心之學，亦嘗聞其大槩矣。故敢陳此，以上酬陛下求言之盛心也。伏願留神省覽，則天下幸甚。臣干冒天威，不勝戰慄之至。臣謹對。
translation_en: …as at the beginning. Yet even with the sagely virtue of Cheng Tang 成湯, he constantly admonished himself with the words of the Inscription on the Washbasin (Panming); and even with the sagely virtue of King Wu 武王, he ever devoted his mind to the warnings of the Cinnabar Book (Danshu). How then can the effort of study and inquiry be relaxed even slightly? The former Confucian scholar Master Fan 范氏 said: "The mind of a ruler depends solely on how it is nourished." Since Your Majesty wishes to achieve the governance of the ancient emperors and kings, how can you not seek the art by which those emperors and kings nourished their minds? The establishment of the Classics Colloquium (jingyan) in our Dynasty is most [宸, error for 最?] close to antiquity. With the Classics on the left and the Histories on the right, lecturing in the morning and reading in the evening, hearing them with the ears, beholding them with the eyes, and letting the mind be leisurely steeped and saturated in them—nothing is more essential than this for guarding against wrongdoing, restraining desires, and fostering goodness. Your servant hopes [領, error for 願?] that Your Majesty will daily attend the Classics Colloquium, continuing the lectures without cease, neither regarding them as empty formalities nor responding to them as mere routine. Cause worthy scholar-officials to be constantly in attendance before and behind, to the left and to the right, in moments of unhurried leisure drawing out and expounding the meanings of texts, so that what you hear are always good words and what you see are always good deeds. Thereby you will nurture this mind so as not to lose its original heavenly nature, and expand this mind so as not to diminish its innate capacity. Then the policies for nourishing and educating the people will likewise continue without interruption from beginning to end, and the efficacy of your governance will grow ever more flourishing the longer it endures. The pivot between order and disorder in the realm lies squarely in this. Your servant's scholarship is meager and shallow, yet having received the Court's education and nurture for years, I have heard the general outline of the learning of the ancient sages and worthies regarding the rectification of the ruler's mind. Therefore I dare to set forth these views to answer above Your Majesty's generous intention in seeking candid words. Humbly I pray that you will detain your divine attention to examine and peruse them, which would be the greatest fortune for the realm. Your servant has offended the Celestial Majesty and is overcome with the utmost trembling and awe. Your servant respectfully replies.

title: 成化十一年進士登科錄
text:
劉戬
臣對臣聞聖人有安天下之至仁有用天下之
大智蓋天下之民固聖人之所當安而天下之
大有非一身之所能獨安也聖人任其所當安
者於已必付其所不能獨安者於人任其所當
安者於已則所以教養天下者有善政付其所
不能獨安者於人則所以教養天下者有成功
然則不自用而用天下實所以安天下也歟聖
人有安天下之仁而未嘗區區自用以安之此
其仁之所以為至智之所以為大而仁智二者
===
之所以相為用也昔禹皐之陳謨不徒曰在安
民而必曰在知人豈非以安民為仁之事知人
為智之事而仁與智不可偏廢乎荀卿子曰仁
而不智不可也智而不仁不可也使仁焉而有
智以濟之則教養之效如炊而必熟如種而必
生如乗騏驥騁康莊而不患不達於其所欲往
矣夫豈有不臻其極者哉堯舜之所以帝禹湯
文武之所以王用此仁也用此智也我
祖宗列聖之所以並駕唐虞齊驅三代亦此仁也亦
此智也曰漢曰唐曰宋所以治不古若者庸非

punctuated:
劉戬
臣對：臣聞聖人有安天下之至仁，有用天下之大智。蓋天下之民，固聖人之所當安；而天下之大，有非一身之所能獨安也。聖人任其所當安者於已，必付其所不能獨安者於人。任其所當安者於已，則所以教養天下者有善政；付其所不能獨安者於人，則所以教養天下者有成功。然則不自用而用天下，實所以安天下也歟！聖人有安天下之仁，而未嘗區區自用以安之，此其仁之所以為至，智之所以為大，而仁智二者之所以相為用也。昔禹、皐之陳謨，不徒曰「在安民」，而必曰「在知人」。豈非以安民為仁之事，知人為智之事，而仁與智不可偏廢乎？荀卿子曰：「仁而不智，不可也；智而不仁，不可也。」使仁焉而有智以濟之，則教養之效，如炊而必熟，如種而必生，如乗騏驥騁康莊，而不患不達於其所欲往矣。夫豈有不臻其極者哉！堯、舜之所以帝，禹、湯、文、武之所以王，用此仁也，用此智也。我祖宗列聖之所以並駕唐、虞，齊驅三代，亦此仁也，亦此智也。曰漢、曰唐、曰宋，所以治不古若者，庸非
translation_en:
Liu Jian 劉戬

Your servant replies: Your servant has heard that the sage possesses the supreme benevolence to bring peace to the world and the great wisdom to employ the world. Indeed, the people of the world are certainly whom the sage ought to bring peace to; yet the vastness of the world is such that a single person cannot bring peace to it alone. When the sage takes upon himself the responsibility for those he ought to bring peace to, he must entrust to others that which he cannot bring peace to alone. By taking upon himself the responsibility for those he ought to bring peace to, there is good governance wherewith to educate and nourish the world; by entrusting to others that which he cannot bring peace to alone, there is successful achievement in educating and nourishing the world. If this is so, then not relying solely on oneself, but employing the world, is truly the means to bring peace to the world! The sage possesses the benevolence to bring peace to the world, yet never relies Narrowly on himself alone to bring peace to it; this is why his benevolence is supreme, why his wisdom is great, and why benevolence and wisdom serve each other in turn. In antiquity, when Yu 禹 and Gao Yao 皐陶 set forth their counsels, they did not merely say "it lies in bringing peace to the people," but insisted on saying "it lies in knowing men." Is this not because bringing peace to the people is the work of benevolence, knowing men is the work of wisdom, and neither benevolence nor wisdom can be neglected in favor of the other? Master Xun Qing 荀卿子 (Xunzi 荀子) said: "To be benevolent yet not wise is unacceptable; to be wise yet not benevolent is unacceptable." Suppose one is benevolent and has wisdom to complement it: then the efficacy of educating and nourishing will be like cooking food that is sure to ripen, like planting seed that is sure to sprout, and like riding a fine steed galloping down a broad highway without worrying about failing to reach wherever one wishes to go. How could it fail to reach the ultimate perfection! That whereby Yao 堯 and Shun 舜 ruled as emperors, and that whereby Yu 禹, Tang 湯, Wen 文, and Wu 武 ruled as kings, was the employment of this benevolence and the employment of this wisdom. That whereby the successive sages of our Imperial Ancestors rode abreast with Tang 唐 and Yu 虞 and galloped neck and neck with the Three Dynasties was likewise this benevolence and likewise this wisdom. As for the Han, the Tang, and the Song, the reason their governance did not match antiquity—was it not…

弊歟恭惟
皇帝陛下以聖人之德居聖人之位寬裕温柔浩乎
天地不足以為大文理密察昭乎日月不足以
為明矣然而處既聖之地無自聖之心惟恐一
善之或遺不以邇言為可忽乃進臣等于
廷咨之以當時之事首言教養之效未臻其極而
拳拳焉以任用未盡得人為疑中舉歷代之教
養而欲考其得失末復欲聞至當之說以教養
天下臣伏而讀之有以知
===
陛下之至仁惟欲以安天下而
陛下之大智知所以用天下也夫至仁惟欲以安天
下而大智知所以用天下則
陛下素所蓄積者皆教養天下之具也舉而措之固
已沛然有餘矣尚奚假於臣言哉雖然謀及庶
人詢于芻蕘古之聖人蓋如此而布衣言天下
事亦有志經世者所以驗可而進以行其所學
也臣又安敢自棄於疎賤而不有以對揚
聖天子之休命乎昔宋儒蘇軾進說於其君以為言
之於無事之時常患於不見聽臣竊以為此獨

punctuated: 此仁、此智有所未盡，或得其一而不能兼舉之弊歟？恭惟皇帝陛下以聖人之德，居聖人之位，寬裕温柔，浩乎天地不足以為大；文理密察，昭乎日月不足以為明矣。然而處既聖之地，無自聖之心，惟恐一善之或遺，不以邇言為可忽。乃進臣等于廷，咨之以當時之事。首言教養之效未臻其極，而拳拳焉以任用未盡得人為疑；中舉歷代之教養，而欲考其得失；末復欲聞至當之說，以教養天下。臣伏而讀之，有以知陛下之至仁惟欲以安天下，而陛下之大智知所以用天下也。夫至仁惟欲以安天下，而大智知所以用天下，則陛下素所蓄積者，皆教養天下之具也，舉而措之，固已沛然有餘矣，尚奚假於臣言哉？雖然，謀及庶人，詢于芻蕘，古之聖人蓋如此；而布衣言天下事，亦有志經世者所以驗可而進，以行其所學也。臣又安敢自棄於疎賤，而不有以對揚聖天子之休命乎？昔宋儒蘇軾進說於其君，以為言之於無事之時，常患於不見聽。臣竊以為此獨
translation_en:
…the failing of not having fully exhausted this benevolence and this wisdom, or of attaining one without being able to advance both together?

I reverently reflect that Your Imperial Majesty occupies the position of a sage with the virtue of a sage: magnanimous, generous, gentle, and mild—so vast that even heaven and earth are not enough to measure Your greatness; accomplished, orderly, meticulous, and discerning—so radiant that even the sun and moon are not enough to measure Your brilliance. Yet, while dwelling in the state of an accomplished sage, You harbor no mind of self-assumed sageliness. Fearing only that a single good point might be overlooked, You do not regard near and simple words as worthy of neglect. Thus You have summoned Your servants to the court to consult us on the affairs of the present day. At the outset, You state that the efficacy of instruction and nourishment has not yet reached its peak, and with earnest concern You express doubt as to whether appointments have not completely secured the right men; in the middle, You cite the instruction and nourishment of successive dynasties and wish to examine their successes and failures; and at the end, You again wish to hear a most fitting discourse with which to instruct and nourish the empire. Prostrating myself to read this, I have the means to know that Your Majesty's supreme benevolence desires only to bring peace to the empire, and that Your Majesty's great wisdom knows wherewith to employ the empire. Now, when supreme benevolence desires only to bring peace to the empire and great wisdom knows wherewith to employ the empire, then what Your Majesty has long accumulated are all instruments for instructing and nourishing the empire. To take them up and put them into practice is assuredly already more than abundantly sufficient—what need is there still to borrow from the words of Your servant?

Even so, taking counsel down to the common people and inquiring of grass- and firewood-gatherers—such indeed was the way of the sages of antiquity; and for a commoner in plain cloth to speak on the affairs of the empire is also the means by which one who aspires to order the world tests what is feasible and steps forward to put what he has learned into practice. How, then, would Your servant dare to abandon himself to his distant and lowly station and fail to respond to and extol the illustrious mandate of the Sacred Son of Heaven?

In former times, the Song-dynasty scholar Su Shi 蘇軾 presented an admonition to his ruler, holding that when one speaks in times of peace and quiet, one constantly worries about not being heeded. Your servant privately considers that this was merely…

臣聞：惟天惠民，惟辟奉天。天之惠民，必擇人以寄教養之事；則君之奉天，又可不得人以任教養之責哉？盖民衣食不足，則不暇治禮義，此聖人所以有養民之仁也；而養民之仁，不過如聖策所謂「制田里、教樹畜」而已。飽煖無教，則又近於禽獸，此聖人所以有教民之仁也；而教民之仁，不過如聖策所謂「崇學校、明禮義」而已。然徒知教養，而不擇人以任之，則小人在位，無由下達，雖曰養之，而民不蒙其澤；雖曰教之，而民不被其化。此所以任用未盡得人，不能不勞聖慮也。臣請以祖宗之教養，為
translation_en:
… because he had not encountered a sage and enlightened ruler. Had he encountered a sage and enlightened ruler, then even when the state was as secure as being bound to clustered mulberry roots, that ruler would constantly maintain the warning against the city wall collapsing back into the moat, trembling with the sole fear that a single word of counsel might go unheard. Today, although the empire is untroubled and my words are crude and shallow, I am fortunate to have encountered Your Majesty's sage enlightenment; thus, what was called "not being heeded" is nothing to worry about. I respectfully bow my head to the ground upon my hands and set forth my views item by item in response to what Your Majesty's policy question has touched upon.

Your servant has heard that Heaven alone shows grace to the people, and the sovereign alone serves Heaven. Since Heaven, in showing grace to the people, inevitably selects someone to whom to entrust the affairs of instruction and nourishment, how then could the ruler, in serving Heaven, fail to obtain the right men to shoulder the responsibility of instruction and nourishment? Indeed, if the people lack sufficient clothing and food, they have no leisure to cultivate ritual and righteousness. This is why the sages possessed the benevolence of nourishing the people; and the benevolence of nourishing the people is nothing more than what Your Majesty's policy question refers to as "regulating fields and village residences, and teaching arboriculture and animal husbandry." Yet if the people are well-fed and warm without instruction, they come close to birds and beasts. This is why the sages possessed the benevolence of instructing the people; and the benevolence of instructing the people is nothing more than what Your Majesty's policy question refers to as "exalting schools and clarifying ritual and righteousness." However, if one merely knows to instruct and nourish them without selecting the right men to take charge of these tasks, petty men will occupy official positions and there will be no way for benefits to reach those below. Though one may speak of nourishing them, the people will not receive the bounty; though one may speak of instructing them, the people will not feel the transforming influence. This is why the fact that appointments have not entirely secured the right men cannot but trouble Your Majesty's thoughts. Your servant begs leave to take the instruction and nourishment practiced by the Imperial Ancestors and, for…

title: 成化十一年進士登科錄
text:
陛下言之我
祖宗之養民也田雖聴其自占而課農有
詔如春雨之涵濡衣雖未嘗家賜而栽桑有
令如春陽之煦嫗臣竊觀
祖宗諭侍臣有曰衣帛當思織女之勤食粟當念耕
夫之苦又曰朕思足食在於禁末作足衣在於
革華靡又曰人之常情安於所忽飽即忘饑暖
即忘寒朕深知民艱百計以勸督之嗚呼養民
之仁根於中而形於言者一至此乎以是仁而
安天下則民生之厚果孰能禦之哉我
===
祖宗之教民也内設國子監以造就天下之英才外
設府州縣學以儲養民間之俊秀臣竊觀
祖宗諭侍臣有曰治國之要教化為先教化之道學
校為本又曰教化行雖閭閻可使為君子教化
不行雖中材或墜於小人又曰君子而知學則
道興小人而知學則俗美嗚呼教民之仁根於
中而形於言者一至此乎以是仁而安天下則
民德之正又孰能禦之哉然我
祖宗固未嘗如秦皇之衡石自程隋文之傳餐後食
區區焉弊精神以教養天下也亦曰任賢圖治

punctuated: 陛下言之。我祖宗之養民也，田雖聴其自占，而課農有詔，如春雨之涵濡；衣雖未嘗家賜，而栽桑有令，如春陽之煦嫗。臣竊觀祖宗諭侍臣有曰：「衣帛當思織女之勤，食粟當念耕夫之苦。」又曰：「朕思足食在於禁末作，足衣在於革華靡。」又曰：「人之常情，安於所忽，飽即忘饑，暖即忘寒。朕深知民艱，百計以勸督之。」嗚呼！養民之仁，根於中而形於言者，一至此乎！以是仁而安天下，則民生之厚，果孰能禦之哉！我祖宗之教民也，内設國子監以造就天下之英才，外設府州縣學以儲養民間之俊秀。臣竊觀祖宗諭侍臣有曰：「治國之要，教化為先；教化之道，學校為本。」又曰：「教化行，雖閭閻可使為君子；教化不行，雖中材或墜於小人。」又曰：「君子而知學則道興，小人而知學則俗美。」嗚呼！教民之仁，根於中而形於言者，一至此乎！以是仁而安天下，則民德之正，又孰能禦之哉！然我祖宗固未嘗如秦皇之衡石自程、隋文之傳餐後食，區區焉弊精神以教養天下也，亦曰任賢圖治，
translation_en:
… speak of them to Your Majesty.

In our Imperial Ancestors' nourishing of the people, although the people were permitted to claim fields for themselves, there were imperial edicts encouraging agriculture that soaked into them like spring rain; and although clothing was not bestowed upon every household, there were ordinances for planting mulberry trees that warmed and nurtured them like the spring sun. Your servant has humbly observed that when our Imperial Ancestors instructed their attending officials, they said: "When wearing silk, one ought to think of the toil of the weaving women; when eating grain, one ought to remember the hardship of the plowing men." They also said: "We reflect that sufficiency of food lies in prohibiting non-essential crafts, and sufficiency of clothing lies in eliminating extravagance." And they said: "It is ordinary human nature to grow complacent in what one neglects: once full, one immediately forgets hunger; once warm, one immediately forgets cold. We deeply understand the hardships of the people and use every means to encourage and supervise them." Alas! That the benevolence of nourishing the people should be rooted within and manifested in words to such an extent as this! Bringing peace to the realm with such benevolence, who indeed could impede the enrichment of the people's livelihood?

In our Imperial Ancestors' educating of the people, within the capital they established the Directorate of Education (Guozijian) to cultivate the outstanding talents of the realm, and in the provinces they established prefectural, subprefectural, and county schools to nurture the fine talents among the populace. Your servant has humbly observed that when our Imperial Ancestors instructed their attending officials, they said: "In the essentials of governing the state, moral transformation through education comes first; in the Way of moral transformation, schools are the foundation." They also said: "When moral transformation is carried out, even those of the humble alleys can be made into noble men; when moral transformation is not carried out, even those of middling talent may sink into becoming petty men." And they said: "When the noble man knows learning, the Way flourishes; when the common man knows learning, customs become admirable." Alas! That the benevolence of educating the people should be rooted within and manifested in words to such an extent as this! Bringing peace to the realm with such benevolence, who then could impede the rectification of the people's virtue?

Yet our Imperial Ancestors certainly never acted like the First Emperor of Qin, who set himself a daily quota of documents weighed by the stone, or Emperor Wen of Sui, who had his meals passed in to him and ate only after attending to state affairs—wearily exhausting their spirits in petty detail so as to educate and nourish the realm. Rather, they simply employed the worthy to plan for good governance …
